\section[chumbar]{chumbar — to fail (an exam); to fill (a tooth)}

\label{lesson:PT-C379-chumbar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to learn by heart, then the Portuguese for the test.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: chumbar}
\textbf{chumbar} — \textquotedblleft{}to fail (an exam); to fill (a tooth)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Chumbei no exame de condução.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I failed my driving test.}
\end{quote}

European Portuguese, informal; in Brazil \emph{reprovar} or \emph{ser reprovado}. \emph{Chumbar um aluno} — to fail a student.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{chumbar} first meant \textquotedblleft{}to weight or seal with lead\textquotedblright{} and is built on \emph{chumbo} \textquotedblleft{}lead\textquotedblright{}, inherited from Latin \emph{plumbum} \textquotedblleft{}lead\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short); how it came to mean \textquotedblleft{}to fail\textquotedblright{} is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chumbar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chumbar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{chumbar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to learn by heart, then the Portuguese for the test, then say \emph{chumbar} again
\end{itemize}

\section[aprovar]{aprovar — to pass (a student); to approve}

\label{lesson:PT-C379-aprovar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the test, then the Portuguese for to fail.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: aprovar}
\textbf{aprovar} — \textquotedblleft{}to pass (a student); to approve\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O professor aprovou todos os alunos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The teacher passed all the students.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Ser aprovado} — to pass. Also to approve a plan or a law.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{aprovar} comes from Latin \emph{approbāre} \textquotedblleft{}to regard as good, to approve\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built from \emph{ad} and \emph{probāre} \textquotedblleft{}to esteem as good, to prove\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[a avaliação]{a avaliação — the assessment, the evaluation}

\label{lesson:PT-C379-avaliacao}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to fail, then the Portuguese for to pass.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a avaliação}
\textbf{a avaliação} — \textquotedblleft{}the assessment, the evaluation\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A avaliação final é em junho.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The final assessment is in June.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Avaliação contínua} — continuous assessment.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{avaliação} is built on \emph{avaliar} \textquotedblleft{}to assess\textquotedblright{}, on \emph{valia} \textquotedblleft{}worth\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{valer}, inherited from Latin \emph{valēre} \textquotedblleft{}to be strong, to be worth\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.

\section[a média]{a média — the average (mark)}

\label{lesson:PT-C379-media}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to pass, then the Portuguese for the assessment.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a média}
\textbf{a média} — \textquotedblleft{}the average (mark)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ela acabou o curso com média de dezassete.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She finished the degree with an average of seventeen.}
\end{quote}

In Portugal marks go from 0 to 20; \emph{a média} is your average. \emph{Em média} — on average.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{média} comes from Latin \emph{media}, the feminine of \emph{medius} \textquotedblleft{}middle\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): the middle value.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[a licenciatura]{a licenciatura — the bachelor's degree}

\label{lesson:PT-C379-licenciatura}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the assessment, then the Portuguese for the average.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a licenciatura}
\textbf{a licenciatura} — \textquotedblleft{}the bachelor's degree\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ela tem uma licenciatura em economia.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She has a degree in economics.}
\end{quote}

In Portugal, a three-year first degree; \emph{licenciado} — graduate.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{licenciatura} is built on \emph{licenciar} \textquotedblleft{}to license, to grant a degree\textquotedblright{}, on \emph{licença} \textquotedblleft{}permission\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{licentia} \textquotedblleft{}freedom, licence\textquotedblright{}, on \emph{licēre} \textquotedblleft{}to be allowed\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
